Vuvuzela Men

By: Tarryn Crossman | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a country drowning under the weight of violence we have to celebrate the people who keep standing up and trying to help

Unique Selling Point:
Isaac is 59 years old, 9 years ago he decided enough is enough he couldn’t just sit back and hear the screams of the women in his community, so he started a group of about 20 men to escort women safely to their transport every morning. He is the granddaddy in the group, the OG of the vuvuzela men
Every morning at 3:30 Isaac sounds the Vuvuzela to let the community know that the patrol men’s shifts have started and then he collect his first group and safely escorts them to their transport. Armed only with a Taser and a flash light he escorts group after group until well after sunrise then he returns home and has breakfast with his wife and see’s his children off to school.
Isaac has three daughters, he worries about their safety and the safety of all women in SA, which is why even if he never gets paid he will keep escorting these women every morning

Paul is 45 years old and last year he was escorting his group of women when they intercepted some thugs trying to rob another group of women;. Phillip fought to protect his group and the strangers during the altercation he was shot in the stomach. But this hasn’t stopped him from continuing his service. Every morning once the Vuvuzela has been sounded he leaves his home meet to Isaac and start his shift.

Although they are not heavily armed these men are feared in the community, as they have made arrests and brought people to justice. They work in conjunction with the SAPS in the area. In order to become an escort you have to have no previous criminal record

Female character: Mam Anna is in her 50 and still works as a domestic worker in Dainfern. She was robbed of her phone before she got Isaac to escort her
Criminal that has been caught by Isaac: Name TBC

Script:


























Time code Visual Character
00:00 Voice over Getting from Soweto to work for those who access public transport means leaving the safety of your home before sunrise
00:08 Macfarlane link They have to be out here trying to get transport by 4am, they risk their lives every day to get to work on time. But groups of men across Gauteng are sounding Vuvuzelas taking on the responsibility of keeping men, women and children safely to their modes of transport
00:30 Isaac and Macfarlane Isaac: At 3:30am we sound the vuvuzela for the people to wake up and know that we are around on the street so a person can come out and go to work... when you spot them, you acoompany them. They know we are around and nothing is going to happen, they can just walk.
00:48 Voice over Isaac is 59 years old he lives in this 2-bedroom home with his family and extended family. There are 12 children living here and only 2 employed adults. In spite of the hardship he faces, every morning he kisses his family goodbye and goes into the streets putting his life at risk for the rest of the community.
01:11 Macfarlane and Isaac walking Macfarlane: so, Isaac, where are we going?

Isaac: we are going to Khwezi. We are going to take these ladies to Khwezi station

MacFarlane: Isaac, how do you patrol? Do you carry guns? What do you do?

Isaac: we use this stuck that I’m carrying, we also use the vuvuzela so they hear we are here and then we have handcuffs but the weapon we use is a stick or whip
01:36 Voice over Some of these men carry nothing but the vuvuzela as the sound has become a deterrent for criminals. They hear it and run away
01:45 Macfarlane and Isaac interview Macfarlane: Before you started this job, what was happening here in the location for the women in the morning?

Isaac: the reason I stated this is because we noticed that when people were walking they are mugged by boys who take their cellphone and bags. They used to scream all the time. In the morning, you would hear them cry for help. I thought I should help where I can.
02:07 Voice over Zanele and Nesta are 2 of the women that Isaac escorts in the morning
02:13 Macfarlane with Zanele and Nesta interview Macfarlane: Hello ladies.
Zanele: hey,
Macfarlane: how are you?
Zanele: our hearts are not okay, when we were leaving this morning there were 2 boys, one was carrying a bag. Oh, but we ran and when we came around the corner there were more boys

Macfarlane: they were waiting for you around the corner?

Zanele: yes, it means they were waiting for us.

Nesta: you walk with fear because when you bump into them you have to run and if you are female you don’t have speed.
Macfarlane: oh, that’s why you’re wearing takkies so you can run fast

Zanele: yes, because if you wear heels you make a noise and it tells them you’re coming
Nesta: even now we just had to run
02:55 Voice over Dudu works as a nurse in Auckland Park she has to be at work at 7:30 so for the past 4 years Isaac has escorted her to the train
03:05 Macfarlane Macfarlane: Before Isaac, how was it for women?
Dudu: it was tough, it was really rough

Macfarlane: what was happening?
Dudu: there was a lot of rape, you know there was a lot of mugging from the park below. There would be rape at the park. In one month three people died in the park
03:25 Voice over Paul has been working with Isaac for 5 years, las year while escorting a group of women to the train station they were attacked and Paul was badly injured.
03:34 Paul and Macfarlane Paul: in the morning when we were walking I was with 5 of my travelers

Macfarlane: what happened? you were walking and then?

Paul: a shot gun went off; a shot gun went off and I looked for my people to make sure they don’t get hurt. People ran and I was busy protecting my people. The gun was going off with bullets

Macfarlane: how many times where you shot?

Paul: I’m not sure how many time, I woke up later. I woke up in ICU. I don’t want to lie to you

Macfarlane: and you’re still doing this job?

Paul: I’m still doing it
Macfarlane: you’re not afraid?
Paul: I’m not afraid
04:06 Link To become party of these community patrol unit everyone has to have a police clearance certificate and be registered with a local police station but other than that these men are totally volunteering their time to keep other safe
04:21 Macfarlane and Isaac Macfarlane: so, are you paid for what you are doing?

Isaac: no, they don’t pay us as a token of appreciation the give us something small they pay is in kind.

Macfarlane: so at least they feel safe since they walking with you?

Isaac: they feel very safe now
04:39 Voice over Most of the men patrolling here in Soweto are unemployed but working with the vuvuzela men makes them feel less disenfranchised. Protecting the community gives them a purpose
04:50 Isaac and Mac Isaac: there were 20 something of us but because we are volunteering and no one is getting paid, they leave. Others join thinking they are going to get paid but they realize no one is getting paid then they stop that how it works. They only continue if they want to like myself and Paul
05:11 Voice over These men and working in conjunction with the police when they catch a criminal the police are called and the culprits are arrested. But they soon see the same criminals back on the street regardless their presence has made a huge difference in this community
05:27 Macfarlane: So, tell me, if Isaac wasn’t around how would it be?

Dudu: It would be bad, I don’t know how they got this idea to patrol. I really don’t know how they got the idea. Crime here is hectic, it’s not a joke but now that they are here it has gone down
05:42 Voice over In spite of the danger, Isaac and Paul remain committed to patrolling the streets of Soweto
05:58 Isaac We are used to it now, we can’t be scared because we are used to this life. Yes, it’s a risk a big risk but what else can I do? I have to trust in Gods faith. I started…. It’s been 9 years that I’ve done this job. I do it out of love we love it too much. If I didn’t lie it I wouldn’t do it all these years
